The chiller is off and sitting in a vacuum. Pull a purge filter, change the oil filter, or take an oil sample from the sump, and the machine draws air in.

A viewer asked how a contractor should set up a kit to get low pressure machines to a positive pressure for service, and what goes in a recovery kit for them. What's covered:

- Why I recommend RefTec gear for low pressure work, where custom built rigs fit in, and why parts and support matter
- Why RefTec recommends hooking the pressurizer to the evaporator: at idle the liquid refrigerant stacks in a flooded or falling film barrel, so the heat goes right where it is needed

queue.title: Uncovering the Root Causes of Commercial Refrigeration Failures
queue.description:
In this live stream, co-branded with Kalos, Bryan Orr sits down with Kalos refrigeration team members Christian Maitland and Alex Orr to talk about the realities of working on market refrigeration systems. The conversation starts with the rapid arrival of new equipment in grocery stores, especially transcritical CO2 racks, and why even well-trained techs are running into problems nobody has seen before. Because these are engineered, built-up systems rather than mass-produced units, the first real stress test often happens in the field, during installation and startup.

 The group digs into where those problems actually come from. Some are classic installation errors, like skipping nitrogen purges while brazing, leaving burrs in pipe, or forgetting that ACR copper plugs sit on the inside of the pipe. Others trace back to the manufacturer: sensors landed on the wrong terminals, swapped sensors that left a condenser fan unable to run, controllers that overheat and reset, and programming that was tested in a different climate than the one the equipment ends up in. With multiple manufacturers supplying the rack, controller, and condenser, nobody owns the interface between the pieces, so startup techs end up tuning parameters store by store.

 Bryan, Christian, and Alex also walk through the root cause process they rely on, which is essentially the scientific method: observe the complaint, form a hypothesis, test it, and then keep digging until you know why it happened and can confirm the fix on the next job. They discuss store dew point and airflow as the most common causes of iced-up and sweating cases, a humbling misdiagnosis involving a transducer and a redundant controller, and the pain of 19-week lead times and wrong parts arriving seven times in a row.

 The episode closes with practical advice for techs. Walk into every store and use your senses, check behind your install team, pull your vacuums, and document conversations with customers when expectations don’t match the equipment specs. Christian encourages techs to share what they learn with peers, Alex reminds listeners that solving ridiculous problems is the job and a chance to be the hero, and Chad’s late addition is a reminder that equipment should be designed for worst-case conditions rather than a design day.

queue.description:
You topped off the oil sump, there is no leak anywhere on the machine, and a week later the low oil level alarm is back. With no oil on the ground, that oil never left the system. It migrated, and it heads for the coldest point in the circuit, which on most machines is the evaporator.

This one works through every way that happens when you do not know the model yet: off cycle migration, an oil heater that is not doing its job, an oil recovery circuit that cannot pull the oil back, and differential pressure too low to drive the return. Then the much simpler fix on DX and brazed plate machines, and why a check valve will not stop any of it.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Why a low oil alarm with no leak points to migration, and why the oil heater is the first thing to confirm
- Off cycle migration with working oil heaters, and why the RTHD is especially sensitive to a small trickle of water through an evaporator that is not fully isolated
- How an overfed eductor loads the sump with refrigerant, so the oil rides that refrigerant to the evaporator at shutdown
- Oil recovery circuits on flooded and falling film evaporators: eductors, jet pumps, and the gas pump style setup Trane uses on the RTHD and RTAF
- A plugged filter drier leaving the eductor, starving the return to the sump
- Evaporator refrigerant level running too low or too high, and why either one keeps the eductor from reaching oil that floats on top of the refrigerant
- Setting the eductor valve, and why one closed too far lets oil stack up in the evaporator
- Why you need enough differential pressure between evaporator and condenser to drive oil return, and how condenser water that runs too cold takes it away
- DX shell and tube and brazed plate machines: it comes down to refrigerant velocity, so raise the condenser pressure setpoint or shut off a couple of condenser fans to push head pressure up
- Multi circuit evaporators where the idle circuit loses its oil while the running circuit keeps the evaporator cold, and external oil separators on air cooled machines that often have no heater
- Why a migrated circuit may need to trip on oil a couple of times before enough oil comes back to stay online
- Why a check valve will not stop migration, and the cost and complexity that come with an isolation solenoid valve
- The YVAA suction isolation valve and the refrigerant migration freeze it was added to prevent, a different problem from oil migration
- VI control on Daikin screw compressors and why condenser fans do more for oil return than the volume ratio does

More chiller training: https://chilleracademy.com

queue.title: How to Test a DC Bus Capacitor Without a False Reading
queue.description:
Your meter reads OL on a DC bus capacitor. Or the number keeps climbing. Or it jumps around before it settles. None of that automatically means the cap is bad. An RTU run cap is usually under a hundred microfarads. The one on my bench came out of a Danfoss Turbocor drive at 8,500, and I've seen them as big as 24,000.

In this one I test it on two meters, one that tops out at a few hundred microfarads and one that reads up to 20,000, so you can see what the meter is doing while it charges the cap. Then the part that can actually hurt you: why the bleed circuit in your meter isn't built for a cap this size, what to use instead, and what happens when a DC bus doesn't get bled down.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- How big DC bus capacitors get: 8,500 µF on this Turbocor drive, 12,000 to 20,000 on bigger drives, and as high as 24,000
- What your meter is actually doing on a capacitance test, and why the display climbs from nF to µF as it charges the cap
- Why a meter that tops out at a few hundred µF ends on OL, and the 0.97 VDC its test charge left behind
- Moving to a meter that reads up to 20,000 µF, and fully discharging the cap first so you see a real field reading
- Why an RTU run cap reads almost instantly and a cap this size needs time to charge
- Static test versus load test, and the volts and amp draw method you can use on RTU caps
- Why pulling your leads too early means you miss the reading
- How leftover charge from the DC bus makes the reading jump around while your meter bleeds the cap down
- Why the bleed circuit inside your meter is built for small caps, not a DC bus
- Using a dedicated discharge tool like the one York sells: insulated handle, clipped across the cap terminals, not to ground
- Checking a 7,200 µF reading against the label: 8,500 µF at 20% tolerance puts the floor at 6,800
- Testing in circuit with the bleed resistor still attached, and why the reading comes in low
- Why a safety rated discharge tool beats a homemade one built from a dead Turbocor's bleed resistor
- Why bleeding it down matters: a short across the bus is a big boom, and the shock can kill you

More chiller training: https://chilleracademy.com

queue.title: Chiller Startup: The Pulldown Setting Most Techs Overlook
queue.description:
The loop is warm, the chiller starts, and every number on the panel moves at once. The compressor rides current limit, approach runs high, and on a variable speed machine the vanes stop partway while the speed climbs. Most of that is what a pulldown is supposed to look like. The job is knowing which readings should settle once you reach set point and which ones are telling you something is wrong.

This one walks through what to expect on the refrigerant side and the oil side as a water cooled chiller starts and loads, with most of the focus on centrifugals. If a machine trips on overcurrent every time it starts on warm water, look at the pulldown setting. Most panels have one, and it may never have been configured.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- What pulldown does at startup, and why capping the compressor at 70 or 80 percent of current limit saves stress and energy
- Why a hot pulldown, with 65 to 70 degree water coming in on a machine designed for 54 or 55, ends in current spikes and overcurrent trips
- The pulldown setting most panels already have, and why it may not be configured on your machine
- Proving oil differential pressure before a centrifugal will start, and why no oil DP means no start
- Typical oil temperatures at startup: about 100 to 110 degrees minimum, with heaters usually holding 140 to 160 depending on the manufacturer
- Why current limiting at startup is normal, and why coasting into set point beats overshooting it and hitting the shutdown set point
- Vanes first, then speed: how a variable speed centrifugal should load, and the Turbocor exception where the vanes start open
- Why staging can take several seconds, or even a couple of minutes, between steps
- Vanes holding at 40 or 60 percent while the drive speeds up: the machine is raising tip speed to stay off the surge line, not running at maximum lift
- How high condenser water with no condenser water relief causes stair stepping between speed and vane position
- Catching non condensables on a low pressure machine like a Trane CenTraVac by comparing saturation temperature to drop leg temperature
- How approach should track load, why it runs high during pulldown, and why high approach at low load can point to a heat exchange problem
- Why the purge runs hard right after startup: it pulls from the middle of the condenser, and the non condensables were sitting at the top
- Discharge superheat on constant speed versus variable speed: 40 to 60 degrees unloaded on a constant speed with the vanes closed, 10 to 20 at high load

queue.title: IGBT vs SCR: What Actually Changes Inside the Module
queue.description:
Open up a chiller drive and the IGBT looks like one big part, with a control module mounted on top and gate pins everywhere. The one I have here is actually three separate IGBT modules, and they are not connected to each other inside at all.

Same basic idea as an SCR, taken a whole lot further. Using a module out of a York machine, I walk through how the gates get fired, where the DC comes in and the AC goes out, and why the IGBT is the device while inverting is the job. Then how the same module can run three separate phases, like the block inside a Turbocor, or get tied together to carry one leg on a bigger machine.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- What an IGBT is, short for insulated gate bipolar transistor, and how it takes the same approach as an SCR with a much more complex circuit inside, diodes included
- Two parallel circuits running side by side, with two sets of transistors working together
- Why a three IGBT module is really three independent modules built into one assembly, with no connection between them inside
- The control module mounted on top and the pin connectors that carry firing signals from the logic board to the gates inside
- A close look at the gate controllers, with more gate control inputs than you will see on an SCR
- Where the DC bus feeds in and where the AC comes out when the module is used as an inverter
- Why the IGBT is the device and inverting or rectifying is the function, since the same part can be applied either way
- The single block module under the soft start board in a Turbocor, and why it is the same three leg inverter with a dedicated output to the motor on each leg
- How bigger machines tie all three outputs together with a busbar so one module acts as one leg of power to the compressor
- Why that spreads the current over three sets of IGBTs instead of asking one set to handle the entire load
- Separate phases run 120 degrees apart, while outputs tied into one leg all run in sync, with two more modules putting out the other two phases

queue.title: How Chiller Drive SCRs Work and What Destroys Them
queue.description:
The SCR is sitting right there in the chiller drive, and most techs were never shown what it actually does in the circuit. The electronics side rarely gets explained in plain terms.

Think of it as a check valve for electricity. The AC sine wave comes in and splits into two paths. Each path lets current through one way and stops it the other way, so each one passes only half the wave. One half feeds the positive side of the DC bus, the other half feeds the negative side, and from there it moves on to the IGBTs. I walk the sine wave through it step by step, tie it back to the schematic, and cover why the SCR has to have its heat pulled out or it fails.

Would love for you to join me for more chiller training here: https://chilleracademy.com/p/intro-to-chillers

What's covered:

- Following an AC sine wave into the SCR and where it splits into two circuits
- What the diode symbol looks like so you can spot it on a schematic
- Why a diode works like a check valve for electricity, letting current through one way and stopping it the other way
- How that is different from a mechanical check valve like the discharge check valve on a compressor, since nothing inside it moves
- Why a full sine wave goes in and only half of it comes out of each diode
- How the capacitors filter what comes out of the diodes
- Why the textbook terms matter less than knowing where the DC bus gets its positive and negative
- How one diode passes the negative half of the wave and the other passes the positive half
- Why what comes out is DC instead of AC, and how it moves on to the IGBTs to do work
- How the schematic lines up with what is physically happening in the circuit
- Why stopping part of the flow is exactly what the SCR is supposed to do
- Why the SCR has to have its heat pulled out, or it overheats and fails
